SAS CU Hackathon¶

Data Science Career Intelligence¶

Project Objective¶

The objective of this project is to analyse the data science and analytics job market, identify important technical skills associated with junior career growth, and investigate personality traits associated with senior professional success.

1. Data Understanding¶

Before performing data cleaning, we inspect each dataset to understand:

  • Dataset dimensions
  • Column names
  • Data types
  • Missing values
  • Duplicate records
  • Unique values
  • Basic descriptive statistics

This ensures that cleaning decisions are based on the actual structure and quality of the data.

def missing_report(df):
    result = pd.DataFrame({
        "Missing Count": df.isna().sum(),
        "Missing %": (df.isna().mean() * 100).round(2)
    })
    return result.sort_values("Missing Count", ascending=False)


print("=== Analytics Jobs ===")
display(missing_report(analytics))

display(missing_report(ds_jobs))

display(missing_report(jds))

print("=== SDS Personality Traits ===")
display(missing_report(sds))

2.3 Data Cleaning Summary¶

The Analytics Jobs dataset was cleaned using the following rules:

  • job_type values were standardized for capitalization and spelling.
  • Missing job_type values were labelled as Not Specified rather than being assigned an unsupported category.
  • Missing job_description values were labelled as Not Provided so that job records were retained.
  • The single missing key_skills value was labelled as Not Specified.
  • The temporary missing_count investigation column was removed.
  • No duplicate records were removed because the initial analysis found zero duplicates.
In [222]:
cleaning_check = pd.DataFrame({
    "Column": analytics_clean.columns,
    "Missing Before": [
        analytics[col].isna().sum()
        if col in analytics.columns else 0
        for col in analytics_clean.columns
    ],
    "Missing After": [
        analytics_clean[col].isna().sum()
        for col in analytics_clean.columns
    ]
})

3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Exploratory Data Analysis is performed to understand the structure, distribution, patterns, and relationships within the cleaned datasets.

The analysis focuses on:

  • Job roles and job types
  • Experience requirements
  • Geographic distribution
  • Salary patterns
  • Required skills
  • Skill-trait relationships
  • Personality traits

3.2 Job Type Analysis — Analytics Jobs¶

The first question we want to answer is:

What types of jobs are present in the Analytics Jobs dataset?

The job_type column contains different labels representing job categories. During the initial data-quality investigation, several variations of similar labels were observed, including:

  • Analytics
  • analytics
  • ANALYTICS
  • analytic
  • Analytic

These labels need to be standardized before analysis so that the same job category is not counted as multiple separate categories.

We will standardize the job type labels and then examine their frequency and percentage distribution.

In [244]:
# Standardize job_type values

analytics_clean["job_type"] = (
    analytics_clean["job_type"]
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
    .str.lower()
)

analytics_clean["job_type"] = analytics_clean["job_type"].replace({
    "analytic": "analytics",
    "analytical": "analytics",
    "analytics": "analytics"
})

display(analytics_clean["job_type"].value_counts())

not specified    12011
analytics         3830

Interpretation¶

The location analysis identifies the geographical areas with the highest concentration of Analytics job listings.

The top locations indicate where demand for Analytics professionals is most concentrated in the dataset. This information can help job seekers understand geographical opportunities and can also support location-based career recommendations.

3.5 Salary Analysis — Analytics Jobs¶

The salary column contains salary ranges associated with Analytics job listings.

The salary information is examined to understand the distribution of compensation levels across the Analytics job market.

Because salary is stored as a range, we will extract the minimum and maximum salary values and calculate a midpoint salary for analysis.

In [253]:
print("Unique salary values:")
display(analytics_clean["salary"].value_counts())

Unique salary values:

salary
10to15    3608
15to25    3281
6to10     2876
0to3      2592
3to6      2239
25to50    1245
Name: count, dtype: int64
In [254]:
# Extract minimum and maximum salary from the salary range

analytics_clean["min_salary"] = (
    analytics_clean["salary"]
    .astype(str)
    .str.extract(r"(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)")[0]
    .astype(float)
)

analytics_clean["max_salary"] = (
    analytics_clean["salary"]
    .astype(str)
    .str.extract(r"to(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)")[0]
    .astype(float)
)

# Calculate midpoint salary

analytics_clean["avg_salary"] = (
    analytics_clean["min_salary"] +
    analytics_clean["max_salary"]
) / 2

display(
    analytics_clean[
        ["salary", "min_salary", "max_salary", "avg_salary"]
    ].head(10)
)

Salary Analysis — Interpretation¶

The salary analysis converts the reported salary ranges into minimum, maximum, and midpoint values.

The midpoint salary is used as an approximate numerical representation of each salary range.

The relationship between experience level and average salary is then examined to understand how compensation varies across different career stages.

This analysis can support career recommendations by showing the potential compensation associated with different experience levels.

The key_skills column contains the skills associated with each Analytics job listing.

The objective is to identify the most frequently requested skills in the job market.

Because a single job listing may contain multiple skills, the skill text must be split into individual skills before calculating frequencies.

3.9 Cross-Dataset Comparison¶

The four datasets provide different perspectives on the job market:

  1. Analytics Jobs — job demand, experience, location, salary and skills
  2. Data Science Jobs — Data Science job-market information
  3. JDS Skill Traits — skill-related traits
  4. SDS Personality Traits — personality-related traits

Combining these perspectives can help connect job-market demand with skills and personality characteristics.

4. Final Insights¶

The exploratory analysis provides several important perspectives on the job market.

Job Market¶

The Analytics Jobs dataset contains the largest number of records among the four datasets, making it the primary source for understanding Analytics job-market patterns.

Experience¶

The experience analysis shows how Analytics opportunities are distributed across different experience requirements.

Location¶

The location analysis identifies the geographical areas with the highest concentration of Analytics job listings.

Salary¶

Salary ranges were converted into approximate minimum, maximum and midpoint values to enable numerical analysis.

The midpoint should be treated as an approximate representation of the reported salary range rather than an exact salary.

Skills¶

The skill analysis identifies the most frequently requested skills in Analytics job postings.

Skill Traits¶

The JDS Skill Traits dataset provides additional information about skill-related characteristics that can be compared with job-market demand.

Personality Traits¶

The SDS Personality Traits dataset adds a personality dimension to the analysis and can support broader career-profile analysis.

Overall¶

Together, these datasets provide a foundation for connecting:

Job Demand → Skills → Experience → Salary → Location → Skill Traits → Personality Traits

This can support data-driven career and job-role recommendations.

Conclusion¶

This project performed a complete exploratory analysis of four related datasets covering Analytics jobs, Data Science jobs, skill traits and personality traits.

The workflow included:

  • Data loading
  • Data-quality investigation
  • Missing-value analysis
  • Duplicate checking
  • Data cleaning
  • Data validation
  • Job-type analysis
  • Experience analysis
  • Location analysis
  • Salary analysis
  • Skill-frequency analysis
  • Skill-trait analysis
  • Personality-trait analysis
  • Cross-dataset comparison

The cleaned datasets and exploratory findings provide a foundation for developing a data-driven career intelligence and recommendation system.

The next stage can use these findings to build role matching, skill-gap analysis and career recommendations.
